summary: Specifies RSVP extensions for a Receiver Proxy that performs signaling on behalf of a receiver that is not RSVP-capable, when triggered by receiving RSVP Path messages from the sender. It is a companion to RFC 5945. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: A helper answers the call for someone who can't, so the reservation is made as far as the helper.

questions: what is an rsvp receiver proxy
what is the receiver proxy control policy element
how does an rsvp sender learn a reservation failed
subtitle: Lets an RSVP router reserve resources on behalf of a receiver that cannot speak RSVP, and tells the sender when that fails.

tldr.problem: RSVP assumes the sender and receiver both take part, and conventional error messages for a failed reservation go only toward the receiver, so a sender relying on a proxy is never told.
tldr.mechanism: A Path-Triggered Receiver Proxy answers Path messages with Resv messages for the receiver, and tells the sender about failures through a PathErr message (required) or a Notify message (optional). A new Receiver Proxy Control policy element lets the sender say whether a proxy is needed.
tldr.outcome: Reservations can cover the path up to the proxy, and can be extended further when an RSVP-capable receiver or another proxy is downstream. The RFC updates RFC 2205.

today: RFC 5946 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2205. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and its companion is RFC 5945.

sections.title: Reserving for a Receiver That Cannot Ask
sections.content:
The Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP, RFC 2205) reserves resources along a path to guarantee Quality of Service, but it assumes both the sender and the receiver support RSVP. This RFC covers the case where one of them does not. The companion document RFC 5945 describes the proxy approaches.

With a Path-Triggered RSVP Receiver Proxy, an RSVP-capable router uses the sender's Path messages as the cue to reserve on behalf of the non-RSVP-capable receiver. Reservations are then made under the sender's control, which changes the usual receiver-driven RSVP model.

The RFC is clear that the strongly recommended deployment model remains end-to-end RSVP. Proxies add operational burden or topological constraints, so this work is meant only for special environments where RSVP cannot be used on some senders or receivers.
sections.eli5: Normally both people on a phone call must pick up. Here a helper picks up for the person who has no phone and holds the line open as far as the helper's desk.

sections.title: Proxy Roles and Terms
sections.content:
An RSVP Receiver Proxy is an RSVP-capable router that performs, for a receiver, the RSVP operations that receiver would normally do. RSVP is used upstream of the proxy and not downstream. An RSVP Sender Proxy does the mirror-image job for a sender. A Regular RSVP Router is neither.

These roles are relative to one unidirectional flow. A router can be a Receiver Proxy for one flow, a Sender Proxy for another and a regular router for a third.

When a Path message arrives, the Receiver Proxy sets up Path state as normal, finds the downstream interface toward the receiver and sinks the Path message. It then behaves as if a Resv message had arrived on that interface: it performs admission control, sets up Resv state, forwards a Resv upstream, refreshes it periodically, and tears the reservation down if the Path state is torn down.
sections.eli5: A helper can play the receiver for one game and the sender for another game, so the job belongs to the game, not to the helper.

sections.title: Telling the Sender via PathErr
sections.content:
With conventional RSVP, an admission control failure sends a ResvErr downstream toward the receiver. When a proxy is the receiver's stand-in, the proxy is told but the sender is not. The sender could guess from a missing Resv, but prompt notification gives faster user feedback (for example a busy signal) and faster release of application resources.

The mandatory method is that the proxy MUST generate a PathErr message when the reservation failed or was torn down and the proxy cannot re-establish it. The PathErr has the regular RFC 2205 format.

  • For FF-style (Fixed-Filter) and SE-style (Shared-Explicit) reservations, the PathErr goes to the sender or senders whose reservations failed.
  • For WF-style (Wildcard-Filter) reservations, the proxy SHOULD send a PathErr to each sender, which is somewhat overly conservative.
  • If the error is Code 1 (Admission Control Failure) or Code 2 (Policy Control Failure), the code and value are copied into the PathErr. Any other error becomes the new Code 36, Unrecoverable Receiver Proxy Error. The error node is always the proxy's address.

For Code 36, the 16-bit Error Value is split into two bytes. If the high byte is 0000 0001, the low byte carries the original error code, which the sender MAY use to interpret the failure. If the high byte is 0000 0000, the low byte MUST be zero and the sender ignores it.

Regular receivers are not changed. The RFC explicitly does not propose that they send PathErr, because an RSVP-capable receiver can synchronize reservation and application state itself.
sections.eli5: When the reservation fails, the helper sends the caller a note saying so, instead of keeping the bad news to itself.

sections.title: Telling the Sender via Notify
sections.content:
A second, OPTIONAL method uses the Notify message from RFC 3473, which can be sent directly to a node that is not an immediate neighbor. It aims to be faster, since the failure notice does not have to travel down to the proxy and back up hop by hop.

A sender that wants this includes a Notify Request object holding its IP address in its Path messages. The proxy copies a Notify Request object into the Resv messages it generates, with one of two addresses:

  • Direct Notify: the sender's own address, so the router where the failure occurs notifies the sender directly. This cannot guarantee notifying all affected senders when there are several, so it suits single-sender applications.
  • Indirect Notify: an address of the proxy, which then sends a Notify to the sender. The proxy MUST do this under Indirect Notify, and its logic matches the PathErr method.

It is RECOMMENDED that the proxy also send a PathErr when it uses Notify, so the sender is told even if a router does not support Notify. In controlled environments where all routers support Notify, the proxy MAY rely on Notify alone.
sections.eli5: Instead of passing the news along a line of people, the message goes straight to the caller, but the helper still passes the news down the line too, just in case.

sections.title: Stretching the Reservation Further
sections.content:
Section 4 gives two ways for a reservation to span as much of the path as possible, whether or not the receiver can speak RSVP. This eases migration from proxies to end-to-end RSVP, because receivers can be upgraded one at a time and then benefit from end-to-end reservations.

Dynamic discovery (Section 4.1). A proxy supporting it forwards the Path message downstream instead of terminating it. If an RSVP-capable receiver or another proxy answers with a Resv, the proxy MUST convert to behaving as a regular RSVP router for that flow. If nothing answers, the unanswered Path messages (sent every RSVP refresh interval, 30 seconds by default) cost a little bandwidth, and the proxy MAY tear down the unanswered downstream state after a predetermined time. This needs no new RSVP extensions. Implementations SHOULD support it.

Receiver Proxy Control policy element (Section 4.2). The sender marks Path messages to say whether a proxy is needed. It is defined for Path messages and unicast reservations only, and support is optional (MAY).
sections.eli5: The helper first checks whether the person has a phone after all. If someone picks up further down the line, the helper steps aside.

sections.title: The Receiver Proxy Control Policy Element
sections.content:
This new policy element travels inside a POLICY_DATA object (RFC 2750). It is 8 bytes long, with a P-Type of REC_PROXY_CONTROL = 0x07, a 24-bit Reserved field (zero on transmit, ignored on reception) and an 8-bit Control-Value.

  • 0 Reserved: a proxy that understands the element MUST ignore it.
  • 1 Receiver-Proxy-Needed: the proxy MUST try to insert itself as the proxy for the flow, and if it supports dynamic discovery it still sends the Path onward. A sender MAY use this when it knows the receiver is not RSVP-capable.
  • 2 Receiver-Proxy-Not-Needed: the proxy MUST NOT insert itself. A sender MAY use this when it knows the receiver is RSVP-capable.

Policy-ignorant nodes and policy-capable nodes that do not recognize the element pass it along under the default handling in RFC 2750, so the element can cross routers that do not support this RFC.
sections.eli5: The caller can write on the call slip either "please use a helper" or "no helper needed, I know they have a phone."

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RSVP apply. RSVP authentication from RFC 2747 and RFC 3097 protects messages hop by hop, and implementations of this document SHOULD support it. Because some RSVP messages use the IP router alert option, RSVP and these proxy approaches are limited to controlled environments where the associated risks are understood and protected against.

With a proxy, the reservation is controlled by the proxy rather than the receiver, so end systems have to trust it. The RFC argues that basic RSVP already assumes end systems trust RSVP nodes, so this does not change the trust model. A proxy can even reduce risk: an operator with senders and routers in secured premises and receivers in customer premises can exclude receivers from RSVP entirely and filter RSVP messages at the network edge.

Notify messages can be sent non-hop-by-hop, which bypasses hop-by-hop integrity. IPsec can provide integrity and authentication for them, or sending such Notify messages can be disabled. The policy element's integrity can be protected as described in RFC 2750.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to trust the helper, just as they already trust the routers. Keeping the untrusted customer end out of the reservation game makes things safer.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA updated the entries for RSVP Error Codes 1 and 2 to also cite this RFC, since they can now appear in PathErr messages as well as ResvErr messages. It also allocated a new error code, 36 (Unrecoverable Receiver Proxy Error).

One P-Type was allocated for the Receiver Proxy Control policy element, and a new registry holds its Control-Values: 0 Reserved, 1 Receiver-Proxy-Needed and 2 Receiver-Proxy-Not-Needed. Numbers 3 to 127 are allocated by IETF Review, 128 to 240 First Come First Served, and 241 to 255 are for Private Use.
sections.eli5: The official lists got a new error number and a new set of codes for the call slip.
